ERDŐS 196: A PERMUTATION OF THE NATURAL NUMBERS
WITH NO MONOTONE FOUR-TERM ARITHMETIC PROGRESSION
JENSEN KOHLMEYER AND LIAM KRUER
ABSTRACT. We construct a permutation of the natural numbers containing no increasing or decreasing four-term
arithmetic progression as a subsequence. This gives a negative answer to Erdős problem 196. The construction
extends finite prefixes while preserving two conditions: every ordered three-term progression with a nonneg-
ative fourth term has that term already placed before its third, and the requirements imposed by unfinished
progressions agree at each binary residue node. To extend a prefix, we order a new finite block by an adapted
binary order and impose saturation only at nodes where the old prefix branches. Finiteness follows from the
weight 𝑤(𝑛) = 2𝜌(𝑛) 𝑛, where 𝜌 is a finite binary residue rank. The extension preserves both conditions and can
include any prescribed finite set. Iteration therefore gives a bijection of order type 𝜔 on all the natural numbers.
The finite extension theorem, the resulting bijection, and the exact negative answer are formalized in Lean 4.
1. INTRODUCTION
Write N0 = { 0, 1, 2, . . .} . A permutation of N0 means a bijection 𝑝 : N0 → N0, viewed as the sequence
𝑝(0), 𝑝 (1), . . .. A monotone four-term arithmetic progression in this sequence consists of indices 𝑖 < 𝑗 <
𝑘 < ℓ and integers 𝑎, ℎ, with ℎ ≠ 0, such that
( 𝑝(𝑖), 𝑝 ( 𝑗), 𝑝 (𝑘), 𝑝 (ℓ)) = (𝑎, 𝑎 + ℎ, 𝑎 + 2ℎ, 𝑎 + 3ℎ).
Both signs of ℎ are allowed. Equivalently, the four values satisfy
𝑝(𝑖) + 𝑝(𝑘) = 2𝑝( 𝑗), 𝑝 ( 𝑗) + 𝑝(ℓ) = 2𝑝(𝑘). (1.1)
Their distinctness follows from injectivity. These equalities also avoid any ambiguity about subtraction in
the natural numbers.
Davis, Entringer, Graham, and Simmons [ 3] proved that every permutation of the positive integers con-
tains a monotone three-term arithmetic progression and constructed a permutation containing no monotone
five-term progression. The remaining four-term question is recorded as Erdős problem 196 in the Formal
Conjectures library [ 5] and on Conjectures.io [ 2]. We prove the following.
Theorem 1.1. There exists a bijection 𝑝 : N0 → N0 for which no indices𝑖 < 𝑗 < 𝑘 < ℓ satisfy both equalities
in (1.1).
Adding one to each value and shifting the starting index gives the same conclusion for permutations of
the positive integers.
Binary residue orders provide an elementary way to order every finite set of integers without a monotone
three-term progression. Related orders on infinite sets are classical; see Ardal, Brown, and Jungić [ 1]. Such
an order need not enumerate its underlying set in a sequence indexed by N0: an element can have infinitely
many predecessors. Our construction instead preserves an entire finite prefix at each step.
There are also strong density results for subsets admitting permutations that avoid monotone progressions.
Geneson [ 4] obtains density supremum results for lengths at least four and explicitly distinguishes them from
an avoiding permutation of all the natural numbers. Theorem 1.1 addresses the full underlying set directly.

The main point is a finite extension theorem. A prefix records both the fourth terms that must already
have appeared and the binary preferences required by progressions whose last two terms are still absent. We
impose saturation at the finitely many nodes where the old prefix occupies both children. After the new block
is appended, the future requirements keep their orientation at those nodes and reverse it at the other nodes.
This update is what makes repeated extension possible. A weighted finite set supplies the needed saturation
without a limiting argument.
Sections 2 and 3 establish the order and finiteness lemmas. Sections 4 and 5 prove the extension theorem.
Section 6 constructs the permutation, and Section 7 describes the accompanying complete formalization.

We first give a finiteness lemma that applies to any natural-valued rank.
Lemma 3.1. Let 𝜌 : N0 → N0 and let 𝐹 ⊆ N0 be finite. There is a finite set 𝐴 ⊇ 𝐹 such that
𝜌(𝑥) < 𝜌 (𝑦), 𝑥 ≤ 2𝑦, 𝑦 ∈ 𝐴 =⇒ 𝑥 ∈ 𝐴. (3.1)
Proof. Define
𝑤(𝑛) = 2𝜌(𝑛) 𝑛, 𝑀 = max({ 𝑤(𝑛) : 𝑛 ∈ 𝐹} ∪ { 0} ), 𝐴 = { 𝑛 ∈ N0 : 𝑤(𝑛) ≤ 𝑀 } .
Since 𝑛 ≤ 𝑤(𝑛), the set 𝐴 is contained in { 0, . . . , 𝑀 } and is finite. It contains 𝐹 by the choice of 𝑀. If
𝜌(𝑥) < 𝜌 (𝑦) and 𝑥 ≤ 2𝑦, then 𝜌(𝑥) + 1 ≤ 𝜌(𝑦), so

Thus 𝑦 ∈ 𝐴 implies 𝑥 ∈ 𝐴. □
Definition 3.2. Let 𝑅 be a finite set of binary residue nodes and let 𝑒 be a preference assignment. A set
𝐴 ⊆ N0 is saturated at (𝑅, 𝑒) if, for every 𝜂 ∈ 𝑅 and 𝑥, 𝑦 ∈ 𝐶𝜂,

Thus a nonpreferred value brings into 𝐴 every preferred value at the same specified node that is at most

4. ADMISSIBLE FINITE PREFIXES
Let 𝑃 be a finite list of distinct members of N0, let 𝑆 = supp(𝑃) be its set of entries, and write 𝑎 < 𝑃 𝑏 if
𝑎, 𝑏 ∈ 𝑆 and 𝑎 occurs before 𝑏 in 𝑃. The notation <𝑃 always refers to positions, whereas < and ≤ without a
subscript refer to numerical order.
Definition 4.1. The list 𝑃 is admissible if it satisfies both conditions below.
(i) Closure. For all 𝑎, 𝑏, 𝑐, 𝑑 ∈ N0 satisfying (2.3),
𝑎 < 𝑃 𝑏 < 𝑃 𝑐 =⇒ 𝑑 < 𝑃 𝑐. (4.1)
In particular, the conclusion requires 𝑑 ∈ 𝑆.
(ii) Compatibility. There exists a preference assignment 𝑒0 such that, whenever 𝑎 < 𝑃 𝑏 and 𝑐, 𝑑 ∈ N0 \ 𝑆
satisfy (2.3),
𝑒0(𝜂(𝑎, 𝑏)) = bit𝜂 (𝑎,𝑏 ) (𝑏). (4.2)

The compatibility condition says that all pairs imposing a requirement at a given node impose the same
requirement. Indeed, for a progression beginning with 𝑎 < 𝑃 𝑏 and with 𝑐, 𝑑 both absent, any extension
avoiding that progression must put 𝑑 before 𝑐. In a binary order, this is achieved by preferring the digit of 𝑏,
which is also the digit of 𝑑.
The empty list is admissible. Also, every admissible list avoids monotone four-term progressions: a chain
𝑎 < 𝑃 𝑏 < 𝑃 𝑐 < 𝑃 𝑑 satisfying (2.3) would contradict ( 4.1).
Let 𝑅(𝑃) be the set of nodes at which 𝑃 branches, meaning that each child contains an element of 𝑆.
Equivalently,
𝑅(𝑃) = { 𝜂(𝑎, 𝑏) : 𝑎, 𝑏 ∈ 𝑆, 𝑎 ≠ 𝑏} . (4.3)
The set 𝑅(𝑃) is finite. Every compatibility requirement for 𝑃 occurs at one of these nodes.
Fix a compatible assignment 𝑒0. We use the following adapted assignment 𝑒:
(i) If 𝜂 ∈ 𝑅(𝑃), set 𝑒(𝜂) = 𝑒0(𝜂).
(ii) If 𝜂 ∉ 𝑅(𝑃) and 𝐶𝜂 meets 𝑆, prefer the unique child containing the old entries in that node.
(iii) If 𝐶𝜂 does not meet 𝑆, set 𝑒(𝜂) = 0.
This definition is consistent. It retains compatibility because it changes no preference at a node in 𝑅(𝑃). The
list 𝑃 itself need not be ordered by ≺𝑒.
5. THE FINITE EXTENSION THEOREM
Theorem 5.1. Let 𝑃 be admissible and let 𝐹 ⊆ N0 be finite. There is an admissible finite list 𝑄 such that 𝑃
is an initial segment of 𝑄 and 𝐹 ⊆ supp(𝑄).
Proof. Put 𝑆 = supp(𝑃) and choose the adapted assignment 𝑒 from Section 4. By Corollary 3.3, choose a
finite set 𝐴 ⊇ 𝑆 ∪ 𝐹 saturated at (𝑅(𝑃), 𝑒). Let 𝐵 be the list of 𝐴 \ 𝑆 in increasing ≺𝑒 order, and define
𝑄 = 𝑃 ∥ 𝐵. (5.1)
Then 𝑄 has distinct entries, has support 𝐴, extends 𝑃, and contains 𝐹. It remains to prove closure and
compatibility. Call the entries of 𝑃 old and those of 𝐵 new. Every old entry precedes every new entry.
Closure. Suppose 𝑎 < 𝑄 𝑏 < 𝑄 𝑐 and 𝑎, 𝑏, 𝑐, 𝑑 ∈ N0 satisfy (2.3). We show 𝑑 < 𝑄 𝑐.
If 𝑐 is old, then 𝑎, 𝑏 are old and closure of 𝑃 gives the conclusion. If 𝑎, 𝑏, 𝑐 are all new, their order agrees
with ≺𝑒, contrary to Lemma 2.3. Thus we may assume that 𝑐 is new and 𝑎 is old. If 𝑑 is old, then it already
precedes 𝑐, so we may also assume 𝑑 ∉ 𝑆. There are two cases, according to the status of 𝑏.
Case 1: 𝑎, 𝑏 are old and 𝑐 is new. Let 𝜂 = 𝜂(𝑎, 𝑏). This is a node in 𝑅(𝑃). Since 𝑐, 𝑑 ∉ 𝑆, compatibility of
𝑃 and the choice of 𝑒 give
𝑒(𝜂) = bit𝜂 (𝑏) = bit𝜂 (𝑑).
By Lemma 2.2, the digit of 𝑐 is the other digit and 𝑑 ≤ 2𝑐. As 𝑐 ∈ 𝐴, saturation at 𝜂 gives 𝑑 ∈ 𝐴. Our
assumption 𝑑 ∉ 𝑆 now makes 𝑑 new. Its preferred digit puts it before 𝑐 in ≺𝑒, hence before 𝑐 in 𝐵 and in 𝑄.
Case 2: 𝑎 is old and 𝑏, 𝑐 are new. The node 𝜂 = 𝜂(𝑎, 𝑏) = 𝜂(𝑏, 𝑐) is the same by Lemma 2.2. Because 𝑏 ≺𝑒 𝑐,
the digit of 𝑏 is preferred and the digits of 𝑎, 𝑐 are not. This forces 𝜂 ∈ 𝑅(𝑃). Otherwise the adaptation rule
at the nonbranching node containing the old value 𝑎 would prefer the digit of 𝑎, a contradiction. The digit of
𝑑 equals that of 𝑏, and 𝑑 ≤ 2𝑐. Saturation at this old branching node therefore gives 𝑑 ∈ 𝐴. As in Case 1, 𝑑
is new and precedes 𝑐 in 𝐵.
All cases give 𝑑 < 𝑄 𝑐, proving closure.

Now suppose 𝜂 ∉ 𝑅(𝑃). The values 𝑎, 𝑏 cannot both be old: their occurrence in opposite children would

The inequalities used in the proof are precisely 𝑑 ≤ 2𝑐 in closure and 𝑐 ≤ 2𝑏 in compatibility. They

6. CONSTRUCTION OF THE INFINITE PERMUTATION
Proof of Theorem 1.1. Start with the empty list 𝑃0. Given the admissible list 𝑃𝑛, apply Theorem 5.1 with
𝐹 = { 𝑛} to choose 𝑃𝑛+1. Thus
𝑃𝑛 is an initial segment of 𝑃𝑛+1, 𝑛 ∈ supp(𝑃𝑛+1). (6.1)
Every 𝑃𝑛 is finite and admissible. Induction shows that it contains each integer less than 𝑛, so
| 𝑃𝑛| ≥ 𝑛. (6.2)
Here | 𝑃𝑛| denotes the length of the list. The lengths need not increase strictly at every step; the lower
bound (6.2) is sufficient.
Index list positions from zero and define
𝑝(𝑖) = the entry at position 𝑖 in 𝑃𝑖+1.
This entry exists by ( 6.2). The initial-segment property ensures that its value agrees with the entry at position
𝑖 in any stage having that position: any two stages are comparable by inclusion as initial segments.
If 𝑖 ≠ 𝑗, choose a stage whose length exceeds both indices. Its entries are distinct and agree with 𝑝 at
those positions, proving injectivity. For any 𝑥 ∈ N0, the value 𝑥 belongs to 𝑃𝑥+1 by (6.1). If it is at position
𝑖 in that list, the same agreement gives 𝑝(𝑖) = 𝑥. Thus 𝑝 is surjective. In particular, every value occupies a
finite position, and this is a permutation of order type 𝜔.
Finally, suppose 𝑖 < 𝑗 < 𝑘 < ℓ satisfy (1.1). The stage 𝑃ℓ+1 contains all four positions and agrees there
with 𝑝. Its closure condition applied to the first three entries puts 𝑝(ℓ) before 𝑝(𝑘), contrary to 𝑘 < ℓ . This
proves the theorem. □
The construction only needs an admissible extension at each step. In particular, it never reorders a previ-
ously placed value. The binary orders serve to sort the finite added blocks; the stages determine the order of
the infinite sequence.
